The letter arrived seventeen years late. The postmark was illegible, smudged into a bruise of ink and time, and the stamp bore the face of a leader who had long since been deposed. She held it the way one holds an artifact... with curiosity tempered by a faint, irrational dread. The handwriting was her father's. She recognized the slant of his vowels, the way his capital letters leaned forward as if eager to begin. He had written it from a hotel in a city she had never visited, on stationery the color of weak tea. The words were ordinary. He described the weather. He mentioned a cathedral. He asked about her schoolwork. But between the lines, in the spaces where ink gave way to silence, she heard everything he had never been able to say aloud... the apology, the tenderness, the bewildered love of a man who understood bridges but not the people standing on them. She folded it carefully. She did not cry. Tears, like letters, sometimes arrive too late to matter.
